title: Async I/O vs CPU-bound work
description: Learn when to use async I/O, when to offload CPU-bound work to the ThreadPool, and how to choose the right pattern.

data.text: Not all slow operations should be made `async`. Knowing the difference between I/O-bound and CPU-bound work is one of the most important skills for writing scalable .NET applications.

**I/O-bound** work spends most of its time waiting for an external system: a database query, an HTTP call, or a file read. The CPU is mostly idle during this wait. Making I/O-bound work `async` frees the current thread to do other things while the OS waits for the external response.

**CPU-bound** work keeps the CPU busy: image processing, encryption, complex calculations, or parsing large files. There is no external wait. To keep the UI responsive or to parallelize CPU-bound work, you offload it to the ThreadPool with `Task.Run`.

rows: HTTP requests, DB queries, file I/O

data.title: Async I/O — HTTP request
CPU-bound work — heavy calculation
Do not wrap I/O in Task.Run
data.text: Wrapping an already-async I/O operation in `Task.Run` adds an unnecessary ThreadPool thread and increases latency. Use the native async API directly.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: I/O-bound work uses `async`/`await` with native async APIs.
CPU-bound work uses `Task.Run` to offload to the ThreadPool.
Wrapping I/O in `Task.Run` wastes threads and hurts scalability.
